runs.summary: Checked the DIFC employment contract against DIFC Employment Law written-contract requirements, probation/notice rules, working hours, annual leave, DEWS end-of-service regime, anti-discrimination obligations, and DIFC data protection requirements. Key issues found include non-compliant probation and termination notice terms, excessive weekly hours without required safeguards, annual leave below the statutory minimum, and an end-of-service clause that does not reflect DEWS/Qualifying Scheme obligations. The document also lacks required sick leave/policy references, does not include the required equal opportunity/anti-discrimination and complaints framework, and contains an overbroad employee data clause missing DIFC DP Law safeguards.

findings.title: Missing sick leave and policies
findings.description: The contract does not state sick leave provisions and does not reference any applicable employer policies, both of which are required in the DIFC written statement of employment. The job description is also not clearly set out beyond the role title.

findings.title: Probation too long; notice too short
findings.description: Probation is set at nine months and allows termination on three days’ notice. DIFC caps probation at 6 months (extendable once by written agreement) and requires at least 7 days’ written notice (or pay in lieu) during probation.

findings.title: No DEWS/Qualifying Scheme clause
findings.description: The contract uses a gratuity-style end-of-service calculation (21 days per year for all years) rather than confirming enrollment in DEWS (or a Qualifying Scheme) and monthly contributions at the required tiered rates (5.83% then 8.33%).

findings.title: Notice period below DIFC minimums
findings.description: The contract fixes notice at 14 days for all service lengths and makes payment in lieu discretionary to the employer. DIFC requires at least 30 days’ notice (<5 years) and 90 days (≥5 years), and allows payment in lieu; it also requires reasons for termination.

findings.title: No anti-discrimination/harassment framework
findings.description: The contract only contains a general statement and does not prohibit discrimination on the protected grounds, nor does it reference an accessible written equal opportunity/anti-discrimination policy and formal complaints procedure, including harassment/sexual harassment handling.

findings.title: Annual leave below DIFC minimum
findings.description: Annual leave is set to 15 working days per year and unused leave expires each year with no carry-forward. DIFC requires at least 20 working days per year after 90 days, proportional accrual from commencement, and allows carry-forward subject to policy (to be used within 12 months).

findings.title: Employee data clause lacks DIFC DP safeguards
findings.description: The data clause allows collection/processing/transfer as the employer deems necessary and worldwide transfers based on consent, but provides no privacy notice, lawful basis detail, security measures, limits, or safeguards for transfers outside DIFC, and does not address employee monitoring notice/proportionality.

runs.summary: Checked the DMCC employment contract against the listed UAE labour-law employment terms on contract form/contents, probation, working hours and overtime, leave/sick leave, end-of-service gratuity, and termination notice. Multiple clauses conflict with mandatory minimums, including probation length/notice, weekly hours, unpaid overtime, reduced annual and sick leave, below-minimum notice, and an incorrect gratuity formula. The contract also lacks required contract formalities/particulars (Arabic/bilingual requirement and key employee identifiers). Checked the DMCC-governed employment contract against wage payment, DMCC contract registration, medical insurance, visa sponsorship/costs, working hours, termination notice/process, repatriation, and end-of-service gratuity requirements. The contract contains multiple direct conflicts with DMCC obligations: medical insurance is optional, visa costs are shifted to the employee, weekly hours exceed the DMCC maximum, notice is below the DMCC minimum, and repatriation is assigned to the employee. It also lacks required DMCC registration particulars and has gratuity terms that do not align with DMCC/UAE requirements; wage payment/WPS and deduction compliance is not adequately addressed. Checked the contract against DMCC accommodation allowance requirements (C17) and UAE non-compete restrictions (C18). The contract states there is no separate housing/accommodation benefit, so C17 is satisfied on its face. The non-compete clause meets the 2-year maximum duration, but it does not clearly limit itself to genuinely competitive work and does not address when the clause becomes void, so compliance with C18 is unclear and presents enforceability risk.

findings.title: Contract language and required particulars missing
findings.description: The contract is not Arabic/bilingual and does not include required employee particulars (date of birth, Emirates ID). It also does not clearly specify working hours/rest days/leave entitlements to the required level and does not break out remuneration into basic salary and allowances (it only provides a single salary figure and states it includes allowances).

findings.title: Probation exceeds 6 months; no notice
findings.description: The contract sets probation at 12 months and permits termination during probation with immediate effect without notice or compensation, conflicting with the 6-month maximum and 14-day written notice requirement.

findings.title: Working hours exceed statutory limits
findings.description: The contract requires 50 hours per week (10 hours/day over 5 days), exceeding the ordinary 48-hour weekly limit, and it does not address mandatory breaks after five consecutive hours or the Ramadan reduction of two hours per day.

findings.title: Overtime not compensated
findings.description: The contract states overtime is part of duties with no additional compensation, conflicting with statutory overtime pay requirements (25%/50% premiums) and the cap on additional overtime hours per day.

findings.title: Annual leave below minimum
findings.description: Annual leave is set at 15 working days per year, which is below the statutory minimum annual leave entitlement, and the contract omits rules on accrual for 6–12 months of service, paying leave salary in advance, and minimum usage of accrued leave.

findings.title: Sick leave entitlement non-compliant
findings.description: The contract limits sick leave to 15 days per year at company discretion and does not include the required statutory entitlement (up to 90 days) nor the mandatory pay structure and notice/medical certificate requirements.

findings.title: End-of-service gratuity miscalculated
findings.description: The contract sets gratuity at 14 days basic salary per year and denies gratuity if the employee resigns before 3 years, which conflicts with the statutory calculation and entitlement after completing one year of service (with only specific reductions applicable in limited cases).

findings.title: Notice period below legal minimum
findings.description: The contract provides for 14 days' notice, below the statutory minimum of 30 days, and it does not include the requirement to provide at least one unpaid day per week for job search during the notice period.

findings.title: Wage payment/WPS terms missing
findings.description: The contract states the salary amount in AED but does not confirm payment through WPS/approved institutions, payment no later than 10 days from due date, or deduction limits and written-consent requirements (except legally mandated).

findings.title: DMCC registration details absent
findings.description: DMCC contracts must be registered within 14 days and include the DMCC license number, employee DMCC access card number, and confirmation of compliance with DMCC employment rules. While a license number is shown, the access card number and compliance confirmation/registration commitment are missing.

findings.title: Visa costs shifted to employee
findings.description: DMCC requires the employer to sponsor the visa, file within 60 days, bear all visa-related costs (medical fitness, Emirates ID, stamping), and maintain valid status. The contract allows deducting visa costs from salary and does not commit to the 60-day filing timeline or ongoing maintenance.

findings.title: Working hours exceed DMCC maximum
findings.description: DMCC standard is 40 hours/week, and total hours including overtime must not exceed 48. The contract specifies 50 hours/week and also states overtime may be required anytime with no additional compensation; it also omits the mandatory Ramadan reduction to 6 hours/day.

findings.title: Termination notice too short
findings.description: DMCC requires at least 30 days’ notice (<5 years) and 90 days (≥5 years), plus written notice delivered to DMCC, job-search time (minimum one day/week), and visa cancellation initiated within 30 days of last working day. The contract sets only 14 days and omits the other requirements.

findings.title: Employee bears repatriation costs
findings.description: Upon termination, the employer must bear repatriation costs (one-way economy ticket) unless the employee finds new UAE employment within 30 days; this obligation cannot be waived or transferred. The contract makes the employee solely responsible.

findings.title: Gratuity calculation and eligibility conflict
findings.description: DMCC requires end-of-service gratuity per UAE Federal Labour Law and payment within 14 days of the last working day (or an approved equivalent savings scheme providing at least equal benefits). The contract sets a fixed 14 days/year and denies gratuity if resignation is before 3 years, and it does not mention the 14-day payment deadline or any approved alternative scheme equivalency/approval.

findings.title: Non-compete scope and validity gaps
findings.description: The contract sets a 24-month post-termination restriction in the UAE, but it does not clarify that the restriction is limited to genuinely competitive work, and it does not state that the non-compete is void if the employer terminates unlawfully or if the employee resigns due to employer breach. This makes compliance with the Federal Labour Law reasonableness requirements unclear and may undermine enforceability.

runs.summary: Checked the shareholders’ agreement against the cited DMCC Company Regulations 2024 articles on company status, registration/articles requirements, licensing, branch rules, naming, continuation, and corporate capacity/transactions. The agreement aligns with DMCC concepts of separate legal personality and limited liability, and it includes a general obligation to maintain a DMCC Licence. However, it contains high-risk provisions that attempt to bypass Registrar/licensing constraints (bearer shares; share issuance in crypto tokens without Registrar approval) and it does not address statutory shareholder personal-liability consequences for pre-licence or suspension/termination periods. Several cited clauses are not applicable because they regulate Registrar processes (registration, branches, naming, continuation) rather than shareholder contracting terms. Checked the shareholders’ agreement against DMCC Company Regulations 2024 (Arts. 25–52) covering share capital/shares, capital changes, bearer shares/buy-backs, class rights, cross-holdings, registers and transfers, distributions, and director rules. Key non-compliances are the mandatory issuance of bearer shares, a non-compliant share transfer process, an unlawful capital reduction clause, and director/alternate director qualification thresholds that conflict with DMCC requirements. Several areas are silent/unclear (class rights/treasury shares and subsidiary cross-holdings), which could become compliance issues depending on future corporate actions. Checked this DMCC shareholders’ agreement against DMCCA Company Regulations 2024 requirements on directors, officers (secretary/manager), meetings, accounts/audit, officer assumptions/disqualification, and DMCCA inspection/remedy powers. The document conflicts with several mandatory rules, including prohibiting financial assistance to directors, requiring a company secretary, AGM timing/notice, IFRS accounting, first financial year limits, and minimum record-retention periods. Several other areas are incomplete/unclear (manager notification triggers, officer authority assumptions, audit appointment mechanics and auditor safeguards, and inspection/compliance-direction acknowledgments), creating compliance and enforceability risk. Checked this DMCC shareholders’ agreement against DMCCA Company Regulations 2024 clauses on amalgamation, pre-insolvency reporting, winding-up (solvent/summary/insolvent), liquidation/dissolution, sanctions, licence suspension/termination/strike-off, and contraventions/unfair prejudice. The document includes only limited winding-up terms (a solvency declaration, a payment priority waterfall, and liquidator qualification) and a basic licence-suspension operational restriction. It omits or does not clearly implement several mandatory DMCC procedural requirements (especially amalgamation, pre-insolvency reporting/notifications, and insolvent winding-up/creditor processes), creating regulatory and enforceability risk. Checked the shareholders’ agreement against DMCC Company Regulations 2024 requirements on (i) disclosure/false information and internal procedures (C33) and (ii) dormancy/voluntary licence suspension (C34). The agreement partially addresses disclosure and privilege, but it omits required no-detriment, anti-misleading, and compliance-with-directions elements, and it includes mechanisms that could facilitate non-transparent dealings with the Registrar. The licence suspension section addresses operational consequences but does not clearly implement the DMCC voluntary suspension (dormancy) process, leaving compliance uncertain.

findings.title: Possible inconsistency with Regulations
findings.description: The agreement states it is supplemental to the Articles but does not state that the Articles/DMCC Regulations prevail on any conflict, and it includes provisions (e.g., bearer shares, no Registrar notifications) that may be inconsistent with DMCC requirements—creating uncertainty under the Articles-of-association compliance rule.

findings.title: Licence-period liability not addressed
findings.description: DMCC Regulations allocate liabilities/commitments to shareholders for the period before the first Licence and during suspension/termination periods. The agreement requires maintaining a Licence and ceasing operations on suspension, but it does not address who bears liabilities/commitments entered into in those periods (or require protections/controls to avoid triggering shareholder liability).

findings.title: Bearer shares prohibited
findings.description: The agreement mandates issuance of bearer share certificates and permits transfer by delivery without registration, which conflicts with the DMCC prohibition on bearer shares.

findings.title: Non-compliant share currency/registration
findings.description: The agreement allows issuing shares in any currency (including crypto tokens) and purports to bypass registrar involvement; this conflicts with DMCC rules that share capital be denominated in AED or other Registrar-approved currency and that shareholding is tied to entry in the Shareholder Register.

findings.title: Transfer execution not compliant
findings.description: The agreement states a transfer is effective upon Registrar receipt and does not require the transferee’s signature; DMCC requires a transfer document signed by/for both transferor and transferee and delivered to both Registrar and Company before registration.

findings.title: Capital reduction procedure illegal
findings.description: The agreement attempts to make capital reductions effective immediately by Special Resolution and explicitly removes the required publication/notice and director solvency certificate process under DMCC Regulations.

findings.title: Director qualifications too lax
findings.description: The agreement permits directors from age 16 (not 18) and shortens the dishonesty-conviction lookback to 5 years (not 10), and allows alternates who need not meet qualification criteria; all conflict with DMCC Regulations.

findings.title: Alternate directors unqualified
findings.description: DMCC requires alternate directors to meet the director qualification criteria; the agreement expressly waives that requirement for alternates.

findings.title: Class rights/treasury shares not addressed
findings.description: The agreement does not set out how class rights will be varied (Articles mechanism or 75% class consent) and does not address treasury share constraints (no voting/dividends; register entry) if the company purchases its own shares.

findings.title: No subsidiary cross-holding safeguards
findings.description: The agreement is silent on DMCC rules restricting subsidiaries holding shares in their holding company (void allotments; no voting rights; disposal within 12 months; nominee restrictions).

findings.title: Financial assistance to directors allowed
findings.description: DMCC Regulations prohibit a Company from providing financial assistance to a Director. The agreement expressly allows loans/guarantees/advances to Directors subject to limits and shareholder approval, which would be unenforceable and creates regulatory breach risk.

findings.title: Secretary appointment disclaimed
findings.description: DMCC Regulations require every Company to have a Secretary, appointed by directors’ resolution, meeting specified qualification criteria, with defined removal/replacement and Registrar notification timelines. The agreement states no Secretary is required and reallocates filing duties away from a Secretary, conflicting with the Regulations.

findings.title: Manager criteria and notifications incomplete
findings.description: While the agreement requires a natural-person Manager and replacement within 10 business days, it does not clearly incorporate all mandatory statutory disqualifiers (e.g., dishonesty conviction past 10 years, DMCCA/authority disqualification, Registrar suitability) and it does not include the required 5-business-day notification to the Registrar upon resignation/removal/death/incapacity.

findings.title: Officer assumption and filing duty missing
findings.description: The Regulations grant third parties a statutory right to assume publicly listed Officers are duly appointed/authorized, and require Officers to procure required filings/notifications within time limits. The agreement does not reflect these statutory positions or allocate responsibility accordingly (and also removes the Secretary role entirely, impacting filing responsibilities).

findings.title: AGM timing and notice too short
findings.description: The agreement allows the first AGM within 36 months and thereafter every 18 months, and permits 8 business days’ notice. The Regulations require an AGM within 18 months of registration and then once every 12 months, and require at least 10 business days’ written notice (unless 95% consent to shorter notice). It also sets written resolutions at 75% rather than unanimity and omits the required minutes register at the registered office.

findings.title: Accounts not IFRS; FY too long; retention too short
findings.description: The Regulations require IFRS accounts, a first financial year between 6 and 18 months, and preservation of accounting records for at least 5 years (15 for real estate). The agreement mandates US GAAP, sets the first financial year to 24 months, and requires only 3 years’ record retention. It also omits required steps/timelines: director approval/signature, audit and laying accounts before a General Meeting within 6 months of year end, and filing accounts with the Registrar within 5 business days after the General Meeting.

findings.title: Audit appointment and auditor protections incomplete
findings.description: Although the agreement requires a DMCCA-approved auditor and includes some report content, it does not require appointment at a General Meeting or written consent to appointment, does not address removal by ordinary resolution, and omits the auditor’s access/information rights and prohibitions on misleading/coercing the auditor. It also omits the requirement for a departing auditor to deposit a statement about reportable circumstances.

findings.title: Inspections and directions not addressed
findings.description: DMCCA inspection powers and Registrar compliance directions are not reflected in the agreement; instead it includes a broad disclosure commitment. This is insufficient to assess alignment with the statutory inspection/remedies framework and may create misunderstandings about DMCCA/Registrar powers and processes.

findings.title: No amalgamation compliance terms
findings.description: DMCC regulations require Registrar consent and specific documents/declarations for amalgamations (including where non-DMCC entities are involved). The agreement contains no amalgamation clause setting out these requirements or conditioning any amalgamation on them.

findings.title: Pre-insolvency reporting missing
findings.description: DMCC rules impose mandatory reporting to the Registrar within 10 business days upon certain triggers (no business/purpose expired, liabilities exceed assets, or 3 months unpaid wages) and require shareholder notification within 21 days when losses reach 75%+ of share capital. The agreement only states a unanimity-based voluntary winding-up and a solvency declaration timing, but not these reporting/notification duties or the statutory effects from commencement of winding-up (e.g., void share transfers).

findings.title: Solvent/summary winding-up procedures incomplete
findings.description: For solvent and summary winding-up, DMCC rules require specific declaration contents, timing options, liquidator appointment at a General Meeting, filings to the Registrar within set periods, cessation of directors’ powers upon liquidator appointment, annual progress reporting after 12 months, and final meeting/summary/Registrar submissions before dissolution. The agreement only mentions a solvency declaration timing and does not set out these mandatory procedural steps or timelines, and does not address summary winding-up at all.

findings.title: Insolvent winding-up and creditor process absent
findings.description: DMCC rules prescribe mandatory insolvent voluntary winding-up steps (creditors’ meeting timing, notices, statement of affairs, creditors appointing liquidator, potential liquidation committee, and ongoing reporting/meetings). The agreement provides no insolvent winding-up pathway and does not require liquidation documents to state the company is in liquidation.

findings.title: Liquidation powers and dissolution gaps
findings.description: The agreement correctly lists the DMCC priority waterfall for expenses/claims, but it is silent on other required liquidation framework elements: pari passu application subject to priority, officer duty to cooperate/not obstruct liquidator, dissolution upon Registrar confirmation, and rules for disposal of remaining property/records (including 10-year record responsibility limit).

findings.title: Sanctions and fines not addressed
findings.description: DMCCA may impose sanctions and administrative fines at its absolute discretion for contraventions. The agreement does not acknowledge this enforcement framework or ensure the parties’ obligations cannot be interpreted to restrict DMCCA’s powers or the company’s obligation to comply with sanctions.

findings.title: Termination/strike-off consequences missing
findings.description: The agreement includes a suspension consequence (cease operations except meeting creditor obligations), but does not cover licence termination and strike-off procedures and consequences required by DMCC rules, including: immediate cessation upon termination notice, continued liability of officers/shareholders after strike-off, personal liability for purporting to bind a struck-off company, and the requirement that shareholders immediately commence winding-up proceedings.

findings.title: Contraventions and unfair prejudice not covered
findings.description: DMCC rules define contraventions and extend liability to persons knowingly concerned, and provide a court remedy for unfair prejudice with potential orders affecting company conduct and restrictions on altering articles without leave. The agreement does not reflect these consequences/remedies or preserve them expressly, which may create expectation gaps or attempts to contract around mandatory protections.

findings.title: Missing C33 required protections
findings.description: Clause 12.1 covers disclosure and internal systems and Clause 12.2 covers privilege, but the agreement does not include (i) the prohibition on false/misleading/deceptive information or concealment likely to mislead the Registrar, (ii) the requirement to comply with DMCCA/Registrar orders/directions/requirements, and (iii) the explicit protection that no person suffers detriment for good-faith reporting to DMCCA/Registrar. These are required elements under C33 and should not be left out or undermined by contract terms.

findings.title: Terms risk misleading Registrar
findings.description: Several provisions purport to allow actions without registration/notification/Registrar approval (bearer share certificates transferable by delivery; additional shares without requiring approval from the DMCC Registrar). These create a heightened risk of concealment or misleading the Registrar, and to the extent they hinder compliance with statutory disclosure/filing obligations, they may be void under C33.

findings.title: Voluntary suspension process missing
findings.description: The agreement states what happens if the Licence is suspended, but it does not set out the DMCC voluntary suspension pathway (shareholder Ordinary Resolution approval, request to Registrar, suspension period up to 12 months or longer as approved, and the prohibition on trading under the suspended licence). It also does not clarify whether it is addressing voluntary dormancy/suspension vs. regulatory suspension/enforcement.

runs.summary: Checked this UAE mainland employment agreement against the listed UAE Federal Labour Law employment-terms clauses (contract particulars/language, probation, working hours, overtime, annual leave, sick leave, end-of-service gratuity, and termination notice). Multiple clauses are non-compliant: probation exceeds 6 months with no-notice termination, working hours exceed statutory limits, overtime is waived, annual and sick leave entitlements are reduced or discretionary, gratuity is excluded, and the notice period is below the legal minimum. The contract also lacks several mandatory contract particulars and does not state it is Arabic or bilingual, which increases regulatory and enforceability risk. Checked the contract’s wage payment provisions against UAE wage payment/WPS and deduction requirements (C9), and reviewed the non-compete clause for duration, scope, and mandatory limitations (C10). The wage clause is incomplete for compliance because it does not state WPS/approved payment channel use, the 10-day latest payment rule, or statutory deduction limits/consent rules. The non-compete clause conflicts with the 2-year maximum and is likely overbroad geographically, and it omits required voiding conditions tied to unlawful termination or employer breach.

findings.title: Missing mandatory contract particulars
findings.description: The agreement does not state it is Arabic or bilingual and omits required fields such as employee date of birth, employer address, workplace location, working hours/rest breaks/rest days/leave entitlements in compliant detail, and remuneration breakdown as basic salary vs allowances.

findings.title: Probation exceeds legal limit
findings.description: Probation is set to nine months and permits termination with immediate effect and without notice, conflicting with the 6-month maximum and the employer’s 14-day written notice requirement during probation.

findings.title: Excessive working hours
findings.description: The contract sets ordinary working hours at 10 hours per day and 6 days per week (60 hours/week), exceeding the general maximum of 8 hours/day and 48 hours/week, and it does not address required breaks after 5 consecutive hours or Ramadan reductions.

findings.title: Overtime waiver is non-compliant
findings.description: The agreement states no additional compensation is payable for hours beyond the schedule and includes an overtime waiver, which conflicts with mandatory overtime pay rules.

findings.title: Annual leave below legal minimum
findings.description: The contract provides only 20 calendar days after one year and states no leave accrues during the first year, conflicting with the statutory minimum of 30 days after one year and pro-rated entitlement after 6 months; it also omits the requirement to pay leave salary in advance and the rule about using at least half the leave in the accrual year.

findings.title: Sick leave made discretionary
findings.description: Sick leave is stated to be at the employer’s sole discretion and does not set the statutory entitlement of up to 90 days per year after probation nor the required pay progression (15 days full, 30 half, remainder unpaid) or the 3-working-day notification requirement.

findings.title: Gratuity excluded entirely
findings.description: The agreement states no end-of-service gratuity or severance is payable regardless of service length, which conflicts with statutory gratuity entitlements for employees completing at least one year of continuous service.

findings.title: Notice period too short
findings.description: The agreement sets a 14-day notice period, below the required 30–90 days, and does not provide the employee at least one unpaid day per week for job search during notice.

findings.title: Missing WPS/timing/deduction terms
findings.description: The contract states salary in AED and payment by bank transfer, but it does not confirm payment through WPS/approved financial institutions, does not address the rule that wages must be paid no later than 10 days from the due date, and does not include the statutory limits/consent requirements for wage deductions (including the 50% cap for debt repayment).

findings.title: Non-compete exceeds legal limits
findings.description: The non-compete applies across the entire MENA region for three years, which exceeds the maximum two-year limit and is likely unreasonable in geographic scope. It also omits the required conditions that the clause is void if the employer terminates unlawfully or if the employee resigns due to employer breach, and it is not narrowly tied to genuinely competitive work.

findings.title: Missing mandatory contract particulars

findings.title: Excessive weekly hours and no rest day

findings.title: No overtime pay terms

findings.title: Annual leave not addressed

findings.title: Sick leave and sick pay missing

Multiple provisions conflict with mandatory minimums, including probation length and notice, working hours, overtime waiver, reduced annual leave, discretionary sick leave, exclusion of gratuity, and a notice period below 30 days. The document also omits several required contract particulars (including bilingual/Arabic requirement and other mandatory details), creating enforceability and compliance risk. Checked the agreement’s wage payment and deduction terms against UAE wage payment requirements (C9) and its non-compete clause against UAE non-compete restrictions (C10). runs.summary: I checked this UAE (onshore) services agreement against the listed requirements for payment terms, liability limits, dispute resolution, governing law, force majeure, warranties/representations, IP rights, and PDPL lawful-basis requirements. The document has major gaps in governing law and dispute resolution, omits force majeure entirely, and its liability and warranty provisions are likely unenforceable or high risk under UAE principles. Payment terms include an interest rate far above the stated 12% p.a. cap and do not state payment methods. It also lacks a compliant IP framework and does not document any lawful basis for the stated personal data processing. Checked this UAE services agreement (cloud CRM/analytics with customer data processing) against the listed PDPL requirements and UAE indemnification clarity requirements. The document lacks core PDPL transparency and governance terms (privacy notice, consent framework, data subject rights handling, retention policy) and permits unrestricted cross-border storage. It also expressly disclaims breach notification obligations, creating a direct conflict with PDPL breach notification duties. The indemnity clause is under-specified for UAE enforceability, and DPO compliance cannot be determined from the text.

findings.title: Late interest exceeds cap

findings.description: The agreement permits storage in any jurisdiction (including US/India/Singapore) without requiring adequacy decisions, appropriate safeguards (e.g., approved SCCs/BCRs), explicit informed consent (with risk disclosure), necessity for contract performance, or documentation of transfers and safeguards.

findings.title: Breach notice disclaimed
findings.description: The contract states the Service Provider has no obligation to notify the Client or any regulatory authority of any data breach, which conflicts with PDPL obligations to notify the Data Office within 72 hours (where risk is likely), notify affected data subjects without undue delay when high risk, and document breach details.

runs.summary: Checked the MSA/staff augmentation terms against UAE Labour Law clauses on written employment contracts, probation, working hours, overtime, annual leave, sick leave, gratuity, and termination notice. The document sets non-compliant working hours, waives overtime pay, reduces annual leave below minimums, excludes end-of-service gratuity, and uses a 7-day notice for staff assignments. It also lacks key mandatory employment-contract particulars and is silent on probation and sick leave requirements. Checked the MSA and staff augmentation terms against UAE requirements for wage payment, commercial payment terms, liability limits, dispute resolution, governing law, force majeure, warranties/representations, and IP provisions. The document specifies governing law (Dubai) and includes basic pricing/schedule, but late-payment interest exceeds the stated legal cap, dispute resolution is left to be agreed later, and there is no force majeure clause. Liability, warranty, IP, and wage-payment terms are missing required carve-outs/details, creating material enforceability and compliance risks. Checked the MSA’s patient-data handling, cloud hosting, retention, breach terms, transparency, and indemnification language against UAE PDPL requirements (lawful basis, consent, data subject rights, cross-border transfers, breach notification, retention limits, and privacy notice) and UAE indemnification clarity expectations. The document permits broad health-data access and secondary uses, unrestricted cross-border hosting, and indefinite retention without required lawful basis, consent controls, rights handling, retention schedules, or privacy notice obligations. It also disclaims breach notification entirely, which directly conflicts with PDPL notification and documentation duties. The indemnity is broadly one-sided and missing standard procedural and scope qualifiers, creating enforceability and allocation-of-risk concerns. Checked the agreement against (C25) UAE Labour Law non-compete restrictions and (C26) UAE PDPL Data Protection Officer requirements. The document contains no non-compete clause, so the non-compete restrictions are not triggered. However, it contemplates broad, ongoing processing and retention of sensitive patient data without any DPO appointment or DPO governance language, which is a high-risk gap under PDPL Art. 10.

findings.title: Overtime pay waived unlawfully

findings.title: Annual leave below statutory minimum

findings.title: Sick leave terms missing
findings.description: The agreement does not state sick leave entitlement after probation (up to 90 days/year), the pay structure (15 days full, 30 half, remainder unpaid), or the 3-working-day notification and medical certificate requirement.

findings.title: End-of-service gratuity excluded
findings.description: The agreement states no end-of-service gratuity is payable to augmented staff, conflicting with statutory gratuity entitlement after one year of continuous service and the required calculation rules.

findings.title: Termination notice too short
findings.description: The agreement allows either party to terminate a staff assignment with 7 days’ notice, which is below the statutory minimum 30 days (and required specification in contract); it also omits the requirement of at least one unpaid day per week for job searching during notice.

findings.title: Missing WPS/timing/deduction rules
findings.description: The agreement includes monthly pay rates for augmented staff but does not state that wages will be paid in AED via WPS/approved institutions, within 10 days of the due date, and it omits rules on deductions (no more than half for debt; written consent except legally mandated). findings.title: Late interest exceeds 12% p.a.
findings.description: The contract sets late payment interest at 2.5% per month (equivalent to 30% per annum), which exceeds the 12% per annum maximum indicated by the cited UAE Commercial Transactions Law clause requirements. findings.title: Liability cap lacks mandatory carve-outs
findings.description: The limitation of liability is very restrictive and does not carve out non-excludable liabilities (e.g., fraud/wilful misconduct and death/personal injury caused by negligence). It also includes a broad indemnity requiring Client to cover "patient claims and regulatory penalties," which may be viewed as unreasonable/one-sided and increase unenforceability risk under UAE law principles described in the clause.

findings.title: Dispute mechanism not specified
findings.description: The agreement states disputes will be resolved amicably and then by a future "mechanism to be agreed upon," but does not select arbitration rules/seat/language/number of arbitrators or confirm litigation forum. This fails the requirement to include a clear dispute resolution mechanism and (if arbitration is intended) the mandatory specifics.

findings.title: No force majeure clause
findings.description: The agreement contains no force majeure provision defining qualifying events, notice and mitigation obligations, and the consequences (suspension/termination) and time thresholds. This is a required contractual control under the referenced UAE Civil Code framework and is important given multi-phase delivery and staffing commitments.

findings.title: Warranties/representations incomplete
findings.description: The contract provides only a basic skill-and-care warranty and broadly disclaims other warranties, while omitting common commercial representations (authority/capacity, compliance with laws, non-infringement, accuracy of information, fitness for purpose) and does not specify warranty duration or remedies for breach (repair/replacement/refund/damages).

For software development, these gaps can cause ownership disputes and third-party infringement exposure.

findings.title: No lawful basis defined

findings.title: Unrestricted cross-border hosting
findings.description: The agreement permits processing and storage on cloud servers located in any region, without restricting transfers to adequate jurisdictions or requiring PDPL-recognized safeguards (e.g., SCCs, BCRs, explicit informed consent with risk disclosure, or contract necessity) and without documentation obligations.

findings.title: Breach notification disclaimed
findings.description: The agreement states the Provider has no obligation to notify the Client, patients, or regulators of security incidents, which conflicts with PDPL requirements to notify the Data Office within 72 hours (where risk is likely), notify affected data subjects when high risk is likely, and document breaches.

findings.title: Indefinite retention and no schedule
findings.description: The contract allows indefinite retention for QA/testing/product development and sets deletion only within 12 months “at the Provider convenience,” without a documented retention policy by data category, purpose limitation, secure deletion/anonymization at end of period, or informing data subjects of periods/criteria.

findings.title: Missing PDPL privacy notice
findings.description: The agreement does not require providing a privacy notice at collection including controller identity/contact, DPO contact (if applicable), purposes and lawful basis, data categories, recipients, cross-border transfer details, retention, rights, and complaint right to the Data Office, nor that it be available in Arabic.

findings.title: Indemnity lacks key terms
findings.description: The indemnity is broad and one-sided (Client indemnifies Provider for all claims including patient claims and regulatory penalties) but does not clearly define exclusions, the procedure for claims (notice, defense control, cooperation), or any cap on indemnification, reducing clarity/enforceability under UAE principles.

findings.title: No DPO appointment
findings.description: The agreement contemplates extensive processing of patient medical/identification data (sensitive personal data) for development, migration, storage, and reuse. It does not designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO) or specify DPO qualifications, independence, and direct reporting line to senior management as required when core activities include large-scale sensitive data processing or large-scale monitoring.
